## Summary (Ask Bunkankun 聞分館君)

T624 (three fascicles, alt. title 伅真陀羅經) is the early-attested Han-dynasty translation of the *Drumakinnararāja-paripṛcchā-sūtra* by [支婁迦讖](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E6%94%AF%E5%A9%81%E8%BF%A6%E8%AE%96) (Lokakṣema, fl. 168–189). It is one of the very earliest Chinese Mahāyāna texts and a foundational document for the cult of the bodhisattva *kinnara*-king Druma 伅真陀羅 / 大樹緊那羅, who plays a key role in the *prajñāpāramitā* tradition. The text is closely paralleled by [T625](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6i/KR6i0262), the much later Yáo-Qín retranslation by [鳩摩羅什](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E9%B3%A9%E6%91%A9%E7%BE%85%E4%BB%80).

**Abstract**

T624 is one of the works in Lokakṣema's reliably attested early-Mahāyāna corpus, alongside the *[Dàoxíng bōrě](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6c/KR6c0003)* (T224) and the *[Bānzhōu sānmèi jīng](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6h/KR6h0027)* (T418). Jan Nattier (2008) confirms the attribution on philological grounds — it shows the characteristic transcription style and Mahāyāna vocabulary of the Lokakṣema circle. Date bracket follows Lokakṣema's translation period under emperors Huán 桓 and Líng 靈 of Later Han (168–189). The text is significant for its mythological-musical material: the *kinnara*-king Druma performs music whose tones cause the assembled bodhisattvas, śrāvakas and even Mahākāśyapa to dance involuntarily — an episode taken in later Mahāyāna exegesis as a parable of the irresistible power of the *prajñāpāramitā*.

The Sanskrit text of the *Drumakinnararājaparipṛcchā* survives in part; comparative work has been done by Paul Harrison and others.
